paragraphs: When an example can have several labels, deciding what to annotate requires more than finding uncertainty about a single category. Labels may occur together, and many possible labels may be rare. This paper develops an active learning model that uses those dependencies to select examples whose annotation should be informative across the label space.

The model combines a Bayesian Bernoulli mixture with a Gaussian process. Each mixture component represents a broad pattern of labels occurring together. The Gaussian process connects an example’s features to the mixture components, helping predict labels even when label observations are sparse. The authors also develop a variational inference algorithm to make inference across this combined model practical.

The resulting predictions include both label probabilities and a covariance matrix describing label relationships. The sampling rule uses this covariance alongside uncertainty from the Gaussian process when choosing examples for annotation. Experiments on real multi-label datasets report state-of-the-art active learning performance, supporting the value of considering correlated labels jointly during sample selection.
neurips-2021-a-gaussian-process-bayesian.tldr: A combined probabilistic model selects informative examples for multi-label annotation by accounting for feature uncertainty and correlations among labels.

paragraphs: Positive semidefinite factorization represents each entry of a nonnegative data matrix through a pair of positive semidefinite matrices. It generalizes nonnegative matrix factorization: restricting those matrices to diagonal form recovers the familiar vector-based problem. These richer factorizations connect to the expressive power of semidefinite optimization and to quantum resources in information theory.

The paper introduces Matrix Multiplicative Update, an extension of the Lee–Seung algorithm for nonnegative matrix factorization. Ordinary multiplicative updates preserve nonnegative entries through positive scaling. The new method uses a corresponding matrix operation, built from a matrix geometric mean, that keeps every updated factor positive semidefinite while retaining a simple implementation.

The analysis shows that the squared reconstruction loss never increases under the updates and that fixed points are critical points. These guarantees describe the update behavior without establishing that every fixed point is globally optimal. The method also serves as a building block for block-diagonal and tensor PSD factorizations, with experiments on real and synthetic data demonstrating its utility.
neurips-2021-a-non-commutative-extension.tldr: Matrix Multiplicative Update extends a classic factorization algorithm to positive semidefinite factors while preserving feasibility and non-increasing reconstruction loss.

paragraphs: Conditional GANs generate samples associated with a requested class. Some designs use a classifier during training to discourage samples that belong to the wrong class. However, this can favor examples that are especially easy to classify, narrowing the kinds of samples produced. The paper investigates how classifiers can contribute without simply reinforcing that tendency.

The authors build a common framework by decomposing the joint probability distribution of samples and classes. They combine this view with an energy-based representation of distributions to connect classification and conditional generation. Within the framework, ACGAN, ProjGAN, and ContraGAN emerge as different approximations to related underlying objectives.

This connection provides a principled basis for a new classifier-informed design and helps explain why existing designs behave differently. Experiments report that the resulting method outperforms state-of-the-art conditional GANs on multiple benchmarks, particularly ImageNet. The contribution therefore includes both an organizing account of previously separate approaches and evidence that this account can guide improvements in conditional image generation.
neurips-2021-a-unified-view-of-cgans-wit.tldr: A unified probabilistic framework explains several conditional GAN designs and guides a classifier-based approach that improves reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Stored activations consume limited high-bandwidth memory during neural network training. Compressing them can reduce that demand, but lossy compression introduces errors that may affect learning. Searching for a suitable compression setting across repeated training runs can erase the runtime savings. AC-GC addresses this tuning problem by adapting compression during a single run.

The authors derive an upper bound on the expected increase in loss caused by compressed activation storage, using results on stochastic gradient descent convergence. They then relate activation compression error to that bound. A preset allowance for loss increase becomes a way to control compression automatically as training conditions change.

Combined with error-bounded compression methods, AC-GC achieves 15.1-fold compression with an average accuracy change of 0.1% on text and image datasets. Avoiding compression-rate search also reduces overall training time by 4.6-fold relative to SuccessiveHalving. Its applicability covers models composed of the layers analyzed in the paper, tying the method’s scope to the operations for which its error analysis is established.
neurips-2021-ac-gc-lossy-activation-comp.tldr: AC-GC automatically adapts activation compression to an allowed loss increase, reducing training memory and compression-tuning costs.

paragraphs: Answering a question or checking a claim can require combining evidence from several documents. Each retrieval step opens more possible paths, while the query may contain several distinct information needs. Training adds another difficulty: relevant passages may be known without specifying the order in which a system should retrieve them. Baleen addresses these problems together.

Its condensed retrieval pipeline summarizes passages after each step into one compact context, keeping the growing evidence collection manageable. A focused late interaction retriever lets different parts of a query match different relevant passages. This supports queries whose information needs cannot all be satisfied by the same piece of text.

For training, Baleen uses latent hop ordering: the retriever itself chooses a sequence through otherwise unordered evidence passages. This makes weak supervision useful even when reasoning requires many steps. Evaluations on retrieval for two-hop question answering and many-hop claim verification report state-of-the-art performance, supporting the combined use of compact context, flexible matching, and learned retrieval order.
neurips-2021-baleen-robust-multi-hop-rea.tldr: Baleen improves multi-hop evidence retrieval by condensing context, matching distinct query needs, and learning the order of retrieval steps.

paragraphs: A vision model can be challenged by translating or rotating an image, or by applying small adversarial changes to its pixels. These perturbations motivate different training strategies. The paper asks how robustness to the two kinds of changes interacts, rather than assuming that strengthening one automatically strengthens the other.

The authors prove a quantitative trade-off in a simple statistical setting. They also find corresponding empirical patterns: training equivariant models with increasingly large spatial transformations improves spatial robustness while progressively worsening adversarial robustness. Conversely, adversarial training with increasingly large pixel perturbations progressively reduces spatial robustness in the robust models examined.

To seek better combinations of the two properties, the paper proposes a curriculum that gradually introduces harder spatial and adversarial perturbations. The method is intended to improve both kinds of robustness simultaneously and move toward Pareto-optimal trade-offs, where further improvement in one would cost the other. The theoretical result is specific to its statistical setting, while the experiments show the tension arising in the evaluated neural networks.
neurips-2021-can-we-have-it-all-on-the-t.tldr: The paper establishes a setting-dependent trade-off between spatial and adversarial robustness and proposes a curriculum to improve their balance.

paragraphs: Time-series problems can depend on events separated by very different delays. Neural networks must therefore capture both what occurred and when it occurred. The paper introduces DeepSITH to represent this temporal structure across many scales, motivated by difficulties with gradients in recurrent networks and the need for other architectures to learn relevant timescales.

DeepSITH stacks biologically inspired Scale-Invariant Temporal History modules with dense connections between them. Each module contains time cells representing events at geometrically spaced delays. This spacing gives time a logarithmic representation, allowing the network to cover a broad range of delays. The dense connections change which features count as the events represented at successive layers.

The architecture thus combines an explicit organization of temporal history with learned transformations of event content. The authors compare it with LSTMs and other recent recurrent networks on time-series prediction and decoding tasks. DeepSITH reaches performance comparable to state-of-the-art results on those tasks and continues to perform well as delays increase, supporting its approach to representing relationships across timescales.
neurips-2021-deepsith-efficient-learning.tldr: DeepSITH represents events at logarithmically spaced delays to learn temporal relationships across a wide range of timescales.

paragraphs: Differential privacy bounds the risk associated with an individual’s participation in a computation. In machine learning, however, privacy protection can coexist with unequal predictive accuracy across groups. This paper studies why private learning can have disproportionate effects, focusing on differences in accuracy rather than treating privacy protection itself as a guarantee of fairness.

The analysis considers empirical risk minimization under two established privacy methods: output perturbation and differentially private stochastic gradient descent. It examines which properties of the data and model are responsible for disparate impacts and why those properties affect groups differently. This moves the investigation from observing an accuracy gap toward explaining its causes.

The authors use their analysis to propose guidelines for mitigating these effects and evaluate the approach across several datasets and settings. The contribution is a more targeted account of how private model training can produce group disparities. It connects choices about data and models to fairness consequences, giving mitigation efforts an analytical basis within the two methods studied.
neurips-2021-differentially-private-empi.tldr: The paper analyzes why two private learning methods can affect group accuracy unequally and proposes guidelines to mitigate those disparities.

paragraphs: Topology optimization seeks a material layout, represented here through a density field. The paper studies the SIMP method when a fully connected neural network generates that field from spatial coordinates. This representation changes how optimization behaves, so the authors investigate the filtering effect introduced by the network itself.

In the limit of large network width, they show that this effect resembles traditional SIMP filtering and is described by the neural tangent kernel. However, the resulting filter is not translation invariant: its behavior depends on spatial position. The paper connects this lack of invariance to visual artifacts and shapes that are not optimal.

The proposed remedy is to transform the input coordinates using two embeddings that make the kernel and its filter approximately spatially invariant. Experiments confirm the theoretical observations and examine how network architecture affects filter size. The work explains a source of unwanted behavior in neural density representations and offers coordinate transformations that the authors identify as readily applicable to other coordinate-based generation methods.
neurips-2021-dnn-based-topology-optimisa.tldr: Neural tangent kernel analysis reveals position-dependent filtering in neural topology optimization, motivating coordinate embeddings that restore approximate spatial invariance.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning lets tasks share information during training, but sharing can also hurt performance. Putting every task into one model may create harmful interactions, while trying all possible task groupings can be too expensive. This paper develops a way to identify useful groupings from information gathered during one joint training run.

The method trains all tasks together and measures how a gradient update for one task would affect another task’s loss. This provides a direct signal of whether an update is helpful or harmful across tasks. Those measured interactions guide the decision about which tasks should subsequently train together.

On the Taskonomy computer vision dataset, the approach decreases test loss by 10.0% compared with training all tasks together. It also operates 11.6 times faster than a state-of-the-art grouping method. These results support using training dynamics to choose task groups efficiently: the selection process observes how tasks influence one another instead of requiring an exhaustive search over possible combinations.
neurips-2021-efficiently-identifying-tas.tldr: Measuring how each task’s gradient affects other tasks enables efficient grouping and improves reported multi-task performance on Taskonomy.

paragraphs: Some search problems need many distinct high-quality candidates rather than a single best answer. This paper studies learning a policy that constructs objects through sequences of actions and samples completed objects in proportion to their positive rewards. Such a distribution is useful when a limited number of search rounds must each produce a diverse batch.

GFlowNet treats the construction process as a flow network. This handles the complication that several action sequences can produce the same object, as with different orders of adding atoms to a molecule. The authors turn equations requiring consistent flow into training objectives, drawing a connection to temporal-difference learning.

They prove that any global minimum of the proposed objectives produces the desired reward-proportional sampling policy. Learning the policy moves search effort into training and supports fast generation afterward. Experiments on a domain with many reward modes and on molecular synthesis demonstrate improved performance and diversity, supporting the method’s use for generating varied, valuable candidates.
neurips-2021-flow-network-based-generati.tldr: GFlowNet learns to generate diverse objects in proportion to their rewards by enforcing consistency in a network of construction paths.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix optimization can represent a matrix through smaller factors, but this creates a nonconvex optimization problem. The paper studies when its geometry avoids misleading second-order critical points: points that satisfy local derivative checks without solving the intended problem. Its guarantees depend on restricted isometry constants, which quantify a structural condition on the objective.

For rank one, the authors prove that symmetric and asymmetric problems have no such spurious points when the rank-two constant is below one-half. A counterexample at one-half makes this threshold sharp. For arbitrary rank r, they establish the same absence when the rank-2r constant is at most one-third; counterexamples show it can fail at or above one-half.

Between one-third and one-half, every second-order critical point still has positive correlation with the ground truth. Below one-third, the authors also establish a strict saddle property for both problem types, which can support polynomial-time global convergence of various algorithms. These results distinguish exact recovery geometry from weaker alignment guarantees.
neurips-2021-general-low-rank-matrix-opt.tldr: The paper sharpens structural conditions under which factored low-rank optimization avoids spurious second-order critical points and supports global convergence.

paragraphs: Missing values can depend on causes that are not fully observed, a situation called missing not at random. Filling in such values without accounting for the missingness mechanism can introduce bias. The paper examines a deeper issue: even a model that represents missingness may not have parameters that can be uniquely recovered from the available observations.

This property, called identifiability, matters because collecting indefinitely more samples does not resolve ambiguity between indistinguishable parameter settings. The authors systematically analyze identifiability for generative models under missing-not-at-random conditions. They highlight that this issue can persist in modern deep generative approaches, despite their ability to represent complex data.

The paper then proposes a practical deep generative model with identifiability guarantees under assumptions described as mild, covering a wide range of missingness mechanisms. Experiments show advantages on synthetic data and several real-world scenarios with missing-not-at-random data. The contribution combines an analysis of what can be recovered from incomplete observations with a model designed to satisfy those recovery conditions.
neurips-2021-identifiable-generative-mod.tldr: The paper analyzes identifiability under missing-not-at-random data and develops a deep imputation model with conditional identifiability guarantees.

paragraphs: An anytime predictor can produce an answer quickly and improve it as more processing time becomes available. This paper explores that behavior through a biologically inspired alternative to ordinary serial neural network computation. It constructs cascaded ResNets whose residual blocks maintain state and update in parallel, while information passing through those blocks experiences delays.

Skip connections allow some information to travel without those delays. As time passes, deeper processing contributes to the output, so the network’s effective depth grows and its predictions improve. The authors introduce a temporal-difference training loss that gives this evolving computation a better speed–accuracy profile than the standard losses considered.

The resulting architecture outperforms state-of-the-art anytime prediction methods in the reported work. It also recognizes typical examples sooner than atypical ones and is more robust to persistent and transient noise than a conventional ResNet. Its changing output over time supplies an additional signal that can improve processing and inference, making the temporal evolution useful beyond the final prediction alone.
neurips-2021-improving-anytime-predictio.tldr: Parallel cascaded ResNets trained with a temporal-difference loss improve predictions over time and achieve a stronger reported speed–accuracy profile.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning often creates several transformed views of an example and trains the model to treat them as equivalent. This paper questions the assumption that every such view should preserve the same useful identity. The authors argue that augmentation can create out-of-distribution views that interfere with learning representations for downstream tasks.

They introduce UOTA, a lightweight latent-variable model that adjusts view sampling. It adaptively identifies the most important region from which to obtain views, addressing the influence of outliers within the augmentation process. The approach can be applied to multiple mainstream self-supervised methods, including those with contrastive losses and those using other objectives.

Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art self-supervised approaches, providing evidence for the practical importance of the problematic views identified by the authors. The theoretical analysis also establishes reductions in estimator variance and bias. Together, these findings support making view selection adaptive instead of assuming that increasing augmentation diversity will always improve downstream learning.
neurips-2021-improving-self-supervised-l.tldr: UOTA improves self-supervised learning by adapting view sampling to reduce harmful augmentation outliers, with theoretical bias and variance reductions.

paragraphs: Generating realistic images becomes difficult when a dataset contains many kinds of scenes and objects. Instance-conditioned GAN addresses this complexity by modeling overlapping local neighborhoods of the data. Inspired by kernel density estimation, it describes each neighborhood through an example and its nearest neighbors, then learns to generate images from the distribution around that example.

Conditioning on an individual instance gives the model a local region of the overall distribution to represent. Experiments on ImageNet and COCO-Stuff show substantial improvements over unconditional generation and unsupervised data-partitioning baselines. The results support organizing a complex dataset through overlapping neighborhoods rather than relying only on one unconditional generation setting.

The authors also demonstrate transfer to datasets unseen during training by replacing the conditioning instances, while retaining realistic outputs. An extension that includes class conditioning provides semantic control over generation. It achieves competitive quantitative results on ImageNet and improves over BigGAN on ImageNet-LT, showing that instance-based conditioning can also be combined with class information.
neurips-2021-instance-conditioned-gan-f4.tldr: IC-GAN models overlapping neighborhoods around individual examples to improve complex image generation and enable transfer through new conditioning instances.

paragraphs: Noise in stochastic gradient descent can influence which solution an overparameterized model reaches. Motivated by empirical observations that noisy-label training can improve generalization, this paper analyzes the optimization effect of label noise. It seeks an explicit mathematical account of the preference for flatter solutions, where the loss changes less sharply around a minimizer.

The authors show convergence to a stationary point of a regularized objective consisting of the training loss plus a penalty for sharp minimizers. The effective strength of that penalty depends on the learning rate, label-noise strength, and batch size. This connects training choices to a specific regularization effect rather than describing noise only as random disturbance.

The analysis also identifies an extra effect of large learning rates beyond the linear scaling rule: directions with larger Hessian eigenvalues receive stronger penalties. Extensions cover classification with general loss functions and strengthen previous results regarding global convergence, large learning rates, and model generality. The stated convergence target remains a stationary point of the regularized loss.
neurips-2021-label-noise-sgd-provably-pr.tldr: The paper characterizes label-noise SGD through an explicit sharpness penalty whose strength depends on learning rate, noise, and batch size.

paragraphs: In repeated games, regret measures how much a player could have gained by consistently choosing a different fixed action. This paper studies Optimistic Hedge, a multiplicative-weights method that gives special attention to recent play. Its central result concerns multi-player general-sum games when every player uses this method to update their behavior.

Under that shared learning setup, each player’s total regret after T rounds grows only as a polynomial in log T. This improves on previously established bounds growing as powers of T, including bounds for standard learners, learners with recency bias, and earlier analysis of Optimistic Hedge in two-player games.

The result also yields convergence to coarse correlated equilibrium at a rate of roughly 1/T, up to logarithmic factors. Such an equilibrium describes a joint pattern of play in which no player benefits from switching unconditionally to a fixed alternative. The result shows how the interaction among players using the same learning method can permit especially fast regret reduction in general games.
neurips-2021-near-optimal-no-regret-lear.tldr: When all players use Optimistic Hedge, each achieves polylogarithmic regret in general-sum games, yielding near-1/T coarse correlated equilibrium convergence.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can collect new experience through interaction or learn entirely from a fixed dataset. This paper develops a unified approach for both cases, centered on extracting more useful training information from experience already available. Its Reanalyse algorithm revisits existing data points and uses model-based policy and value improvement operations to produce improved training targets.

The authors combine Reanalyse with MuZero to create MuZero Unplugged. Recomputing targets allows the algorithm to use planning with a learned model across data budgets differing by several orders of magnitude. It can also operate without new environment interactions, and the proposed algorithm requires no special adaptations for offline or off-policy learning.

The reported results set new state-of-the-art performance on Atari in the standard 200-million-frame online setting and on the RL Unplugged offline benchmark. These findings support the usefulness of revisiting stored experience with improved model-based targets. The same overall algorithm succeeds in both evaluated regimes, connecting online learning and fixed-dataset learning through a shared planning-based training procedure.
neurips-2021-online-and-offline-reinforc.tldr: MuZero Unplugged uses Reanalyse to improve targets for stored experience, achieving strong online and offline reinforcement learning with one algorithm.

paragraphs: Policy finetuning asks how online reinforcement learning benefits from access to a useful reference policy. The paper studies episodic decision processes, measuring the reference policy’s relationship to an optimal policy through a concentrability coefficient. This gives a quantitative way to ask whether existing behavior provides enough relevant experience to support improvement.

The authors analyze an offline reduction: execute the reference policy, collect data, and optimize a policy offline. Its episode requirement matches the lower bound in the studied offline setting, up to logarithmic factors. A further lower bound applies even to finetuning algorithms that explore adaptively. In this setting, the optimal sample-complexity choice is either that offline reduction or purely online learning that ignores the reference policy.

A different conclusion holds when the reference policy provides the required coverage only through part of an episode. For this relaxed setting, the authors design a hybrid algorithm with better sample complexity than both plain alternatives. The results explain how the form of available coverage determines the benefit of combining offline and online learning.
neurips-2021-policy-finetuning-bridging-.tldr: The paper characterizes when a reference policy improves learning efficiency and when partial coverage makes hybrid offline–online finetuning advantageous.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised semantic segmentation tries to locate objects pixel by pixel using only image-level class labels. A classifier can recognize an object from a small distinctive part, so its localization map may omit much of the object. This paper interprets that behavior through an information bottleneck at the network’s final sigmoid or softmax activation.

The authors argue that this final activation restricts how much task-relevant information reaches the output. After supporting the interpretation with a simulated toy experiment, they propose removing the final activation to reduce the bottleneck. They also introduce a pooling method that encourages less discriminative object regions to contribute to classification.

Together, the changes aim to make classification retain evidence from more of the object, improving the maps used for segmentation. Experiments on PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO 2014 show significantly better localization maps and report new state-of-the-art weakly supervised segmentation performance. The findings connect a simple change in information transmission to more complete spatial localization from class-level supervision.
neurips-2021-reducing-information-bottle.tldr: Removing the final classification activation and changing pooling improves object localization for segmentation learned from image-level labels.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning encourages representations to connect related image views and distinguish unrelated ones. Yet convolutional networks can rely heavily on low-level features that people do not regard as meaningful. This paper investigates whether carefully constructed negative examples can reduce that dependence and produce representations that generalize more robustly.

Positive pairs usually retain semantic content while changing superficial details. The authors reverse that idea for negatives: preserve superficial features while diminishing semantic content. They develop texture-based and patch-based augmentations to create these examples. The resulting training signal helps the model distinguish shared surface properties from the information that should make images semantically related.

Experiments show better generalization, especially outside the training domain. The analysis also complicates any simple preference for shape over texture: texture is indispensable for recognizing some ImageNet categories, particularly finer classes. Models’ relative preferences for texture and shape are useful in different ways under different test conditions. The findings therefore support carefully designed negatives while showing that robustness does not amount to discarding texture altogether.
neurips-2021-robust-contrastive-learning.tldr: Negatives that retain superficial image features while weakening semantics improve contrastive representations, especially for out-of-domain generalization.

paragraphs: Why does stochastic gradient descent learn well, and can its behavior be explained simply by an implicit regularizer? This paper examines that question in stochastic convex optimization. It shows that for every regularizer there is a problem where regularized empirical risk minimization fails to learn, ruling out that form of universal explanation for SGD’s success.

The authors also separate SGD from gradient descent on empirical loss. They construct a problem where gradient descent has a worse sample-complexity rate regardless of its step size or iteration count. This establishes that the distinction between these learning procedures can affect statistical efficiency, beyond how quickly they optimize training loss.

For a practical multi-epoch SGD variant, they prove worst-case performance at least as good as single-pass SGD, with substantial improvements on some problems. Further results extend the separation from regularized empirical risk minimization beyond the convex setting and separate SGD from empirical risk minimization for two-layer diagonal neural networks. These constructions clarify which explanations and comparisons hold across different learning settings.
neurips-2021-sgd-the-role-of-implicit-re.tldr: The paper establishes limits of regularization-based explanations for SGD and proves advantages over empirical gradient descent and, on some problems, single-pass training.

paragraphs: A stochastic bandit learner repeatedly chooses among actions with uncertain rewards. This paper considers a setting where additional variables related to those rewards are available and their means are already known from historical data. In applications such as queues and wireless networks, rewards can depend on external variables that supply this kind of information.

The authors use these variables as control variates to reduce the variance of estimated mean rewards. More precise estimates lead to tighter confidence bounds. They incorporate this idea into UCB-CV, an upper-confidence-bound algorithm, and derive regret bounds in terms of the correlation between rewards and control variates when they jointly follow a multivariate normal distribution.

The approach is also extended to other distributions through resampling methods, including jackknifing and splitting. Synthetic experiments validate the proposed algorithms’ performance guarantees. The work shows how auxiliary information with known means can improve reward estimation and action selection, while making the strength of the theoretical benefit depend explicitly on the relationship between that information and the rewards.
neurips-2021-stochastic-multi-armed-band.tldr: UCB-CV uses auxiliary variables with known means to reduce reward-estimation variance and improve bandit learning.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation predicts how a new decision policy would perform using data collected under another policy. Many methods focus on expected return, which summarizes average performance. This paper takes steps toward a broader estimator that can describe multiple aspects of the return distribution and attach high-confidence bounds to those estimates.

The proposed estimator, UnO, is used to estimate and simultaneously bound the mean, variance, median and other quantiles, inter-quantile range, conditional value at risk, and the full cumulative distribution. These quantities describe different aspects of outcomes, including their spread and unfavorable tail, giving a fuller picture than the average alone.

The paper also discusses applicability across fully and partially observable settings, including unobserved confounders, as well as Markovian and non-Markovian processes. Other settings considered include stationary environments, smooth non-stationarity, and discrete distribution shifts. The contribution is a distribution-focused approach to counterfactual policy assessment, with the abstract presenting these broader settings as applicability discussions alongside the demonstrated estimation and bounding capabilities.
neurips-2021-universal-off-policy-evalua.tldr: UnO broadens off-policy evaluation from average return to distributional quantities with simultaneous high-confidence bounds.
